paras: The lynching of Eugene Greene was the seizure and reported hanging of a young Black man taken by a band of men from the jail at Belzoni, Mississippi, early on Sunday, March 2, 1919, while he was held on a charge of shooting the town marshal. The Jackson Daily News, mocking an inquiry from the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, wrote that he had been hanged and his body thrown into the Yazoo River, and the county sheriff was later tried for contempt over his loss.

According to a Belzoni dispatch dated March 10, Greene was arrested at Jackson on a charge of having shot Marshal Hagan of Belzoni, and Sheriff O. J. Turner lodged him in the Belzoni jail on Saturday morning. No threats had been made, the dispatch said, so no unusual precautions were taken.

Jailer Cummings said he woke about 2 a.m. Sunday to the sound of "a band of men breaking in a door," found the lights out, and could not stop them taking Greene from his cell. Despite a search by the sheriff, no trace of the mob or of Greene had been found eight days later. On March 8 the NAACP's secretary, John R. Shillady, telegraphed Governor Theodore G. Bilbo and Sheriff Turner asking whether Greene had been lynched.

The next day the Jackson Daily News noted that the governor was away and the telegram unanswered, adding that Greene "was 'advanced' all right from the end of a rope" and his body thrown into the Yazoo to save burial expenses. An anonymous correspondent mailed the clipping to the NAACP with a penciled memo offering "the size of the rope and exact location of where this coon was hung." In late April the remains were reported not yet recovered.

In April Sheriff Turner was arraigned at Jackson for contempt of court for failing to produce Greene in habeas corpus proceedings, and he filed an affidavit saying the prisoner had been taken without his knowledge. An Associated Negro Press dispatch of April 15 reported that sentiment was strongly against him. The New York Age, quoting the Jackson Clarion-Ledger, wrote that Turner was notified when the mob reached the jail, arrived only after the prisoner was gone though sawing off the locks took thirty or forty minutes, did not wake the jailer or pursue the mob, and went home to sleep. The judge held that he had failed in his duty, leaving the contempt question for later; no ruling, arrest of mob members or inquest appears in the coverage.

The Black weeklies learned of the case through NAACP releases and the Associated Negro Press, and knew the Mississippi papers only by quotation. The Cleveland Advocate ran the Belzoni dispatch as "Race Man Disappears; In the Hands of Mob," while the NAACP telegrams appeared in the Afro-American, the Washington Bee and the Dallas Express. The release on the Daily News clipping ran from March 21 to March 29 in the Iowa Bystander, St. Louis Argus, Omaha Monitor, Washington Bee and Wisconsin Weekly Blade.

Editors added their own headlines: the Afro-American's "Green 'Advanced' by Mississippi Crackers," the Bee's "Southern Brutality," and the Bystander's description of the clipping as the typical answer of the Southern "cracker." An Afro-American editorial said the "Southern Crackers in Mississippi" "glory in their own thirst for blood" and urged Black Mississippians to buy guns or leave, recommending the former. In May the New York Age, under the heading "Contempt," said the sheriff's conduct showed "the contempt of law and order" in that part of Mississippi. The ANP brief on the sheriff's trial ran in the Black Dispatch, St. Louis Argus, Cleveland Advocate and Dallas Express.

Accounts of the night differ: the jailer said he was awakened and resisted, the Clarion-Ledger account said the sheriff was notified and did not wake the jailer, and Turner swore he knew nothing of it. Most reports date the seizure to March 2, but one Afro-American brief gives March 1, and the Wisconsin Weekly Blade put the body in the Mississippi River rather than the Yazoo. One Afro-American copy dates the clipping March 2 and names the town "Boltoni," where other copies give March 9 and Belzoni.

reader.title: Lynching of Eugene Greene
bases: A band of men broke into the Belzoni jail and took Greene, held on a charge of shooting a marshal, and the Jackson Daily News and later reports said he was hanged and his body thrown into a river (A2, A6, A21).

A 'band of men' or 'mob' took Greene from jail while he was held on a charge of shooting Marshal Hagan (A2, A3); the Jackson Daily News as quoted said he was hanged and thrown into the Yazoo, and later reports call it a lynching, though the body was not recovered (A6, A21, A16).

The jail break-in is reported in a Belzoni dispatch citing the jailer and in NAACP telegrams citing Memphis papers (A2, A3), the killing in the quoted Jackson Daily News and Clarion-Ledger and in reports of the sheriff's contempt case (A6, A22, A15, A21).

framing.detail: Afro-American headline 'Green "Advanced" by Mississippi Crackers' and an editorial likening the mob to the 'Huns' and urging Black Mississippians to arm or leave.
Iowa Bystander headed the NAACP release as the 'typical answer' of the Southern 'cracker'; the Washington Bee as 'Southern Brutality.'
Cleveland Advocate ran the Belzoni dispatch plainly as 'Race Man Disappears; In the Hands of Mob.'
New York Age editorial 'Contempt' said the Daily News comment and the sheriff's conduct showed contempt of law and order.

versions.value: Jailer awakened by the break-in and resisted
Sheriff notified when the mob reached the jail; did not wake the jailer
Prisoner taken without the sheriff's knowledge (his affidavit)

conflicts.note: The jailer's and sheriff's versions are their own; the Clarion-Ledger account, quoted only by the New York Age, contradicts the sheriff's affidavit.
The March 2 date comes from the near-contemporary dispatch and NAACP telegrams; the March 1 in a short April brief is likely a slip.
The clipping answered a telegram sent March 8, so March 9 fits; the March 2 in one copy is likely a transcription error.
The Yazoo comes from the quoted Daily News text; the Mississippi from a later brief.
The variants are OCR or transcription errors for Belzoni in Afro-American copies.

March 9 is the date of the Daily News clipping, not of the lynching; the removal from jail was early Sunday, March 2 (one brief says March 1)
